Lepton. Leptons are fundamental fermions that do not participate in the strong nuclear force. They include the electron, muon, tau, and their corresponding neutrinos. Leptons have spin one-half and form one of the two primary matter constituents in the Standard Model, distinguished from quarks by their lack of color charge.

Six flavors of leptons exist. The charged leptons are the electron, muon, and tau, each paired with its own neutrino: the electron neutrino, muon neutrino, and tau neutrino. All leptons are spin one-half fermions that obey the Pauli exclusion principle. The electrically charged leptons couple to the electromagnetic force via photon exchange, while neutrinos are nearly massless and interact only via the weak force, carrying lepton number through all interactions. These particles are organized in three generations, each with a heavier charged lepton. Lepton number is conserved in all Standard Model interactions. Leptons interact via electroweak and weak nuclear forces, but they do not interact via the strong force.

Leptons occupy a unique place in the Standard Model as the only fundamental matter particles without color charge. They are essential to atomic structure, with electrons forming the outer shells of atoms. The discovery of lepton flavor violations and neutrino oscillations revealed that leptons are not as immutable as initially believed, revealing new physics beyond the original Standard Model framework.
